Sunday 11/7
I learned today that I came though on probably the last car to get
through from Nanking and there are no more going back.
The Japanese have launched
troops on the north side of Hangchow Bay near
and are pushing towards the
Whangpoo so as to completely cirele Shanghai. I have to be back in Nanking Tea-
nesday and I have no idea how to get through. I may try to get through on a mail
boat up the Grand Canal if they are still going on if I can, otake a steamer from
Shanghai around Woogsung up the Yangtze to Nantung on the north side of the river.
From there get a bus to take me about eighty miles up the river to a point about
opposite Chekiang and above the blockade. From thare I can get a boat to Nanking.
It takes two days but should be fun.
I saw Hank Jarrell the other day. He has gone to Nanking the way I de-
scribed. He and McHugh left this morning.
I had lunch today with Johnnie Beaumont
and am having dinner tonight with him and some others. I had dinner last night
with Ki Chun. They both sent you many messages. Ki showed me some movies of the
war including one taken imnediately after the Wing On bombing and showed the clean-
ing up, arms, legs, hands, bodies, simply awful!
If you don't want to raise your
boy to be a soldier then we must be prepared to joint against nations who start
such aggres ions. I cannot see any othet-solution. It is as necessary as a police
force and our on Gimen. I don't want any more wars but I would rather face it
again then see little Bondie have to go through what I have seen because his elders
diân't have the intelligence end courage to put a stop to it. It can be done but
As I sit here and write it is seven P.M. piten dark outside, raining and
drenry and every now and then the vindows rattle and there is a big boom of artillery
and then there is a tat tat tat of machine gun fire, but on the whole it is very
quiet tonight.
hat a mess.
I hope the Japanese are getting slaughtered. Un-
tortunately, I keare they are not.
The Chinese have their faults but they didn't
start and didnt want this war.
Our position is so bad just now something has to be done. Ki Chun saw
I.V. just before I arrived, at the request of Bix, by letter. T.V. told Ki he had
no desire to do anything for us. I have had a long talk with M.Y. He felt the same
at first but I am sure I have changed his opinion some. I asked him what he would
have thought if the U. Government had turned thumbs down on China over the bombing
of the Hoover.
I told him I knew the U.S. Government and people would approve of
P.A.A.'s actions in refusing to fly.
The U.S. had ordered Robert Dollar boats
and all American boats not to go to Shanghai, but the Chinese were not agnry with
Robert Dollar and that our actions were exactly te same and we had no choice at
that time until the position of our government took form as it was now doing.
I told him I thought the uninformed Chinese had a right to feel strongly against is
but the present attitude of the informed Chinese officials towards us was wholly
I told him I believed both he and Mr. Sung knew of my efforts and feeling
regarding China and believed in my sincerity, but I wanted to tell him and would
tell I.V. that the present at itude of the Ministry of C. was such that I did not
enre to work for them.

Chinese people, but I would not consider myself a part of the Chinese government,
